title: The Alphabet of God's Word
sum: Psalm 119 (Greek and Latin Psalm 118) is the longest psalm and the longest chapter in the Bible: 176 verses in 22 stanzas of eight lines, one stanza for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with every line of a stanza beginning with that letter. Almost every verse names God's teaching with one of eight words: law, decrees, orders, rules, commands, rulings, word and saying. The speaker loves this teaching, ponders it day and night, and asks again and again to be taught it.

It is not a calm lecture. After three opening verses of blessing, the whole poem is spoken to God by someone in trouble: mocked by the arrogant, hunted by officials, worn out with waiting, his life in his hand. He holds on to God's word as the thing that keeps him alive ("give me life", nine times). The poem ends not in triumph but with a confession: "I have wandered like a sheep that is lost; come looking for your servant" (119:176).
readings: A single voice speaks to God from start to finish, in danger and in hope. On this reading the psalm is a long lament and song of trust, its alphabet a way of saying everything from A to Z. The many complaints (119:81–88) and the closing cry (119:176) are the heart of it.

The acrostic, the eight words and the repeated requests to be taught suggest a school text: a model of how a student of the law prays, written to be learned by heart. On this reading the speaker is the ideal Torah student, and the troubles are the testing every faithful learner meets (119:9, 99–100).

The speaker is a foreigner on earth (119:19), lives as a guest (119:54), has no land but the LORD and his decrees (119:57, 111) and is pressed by foreign officials. Some readers hear Israel in exile or under foreign rule, keeping the law when temple and land are gone.

views.H: The psalm has no title. Jewish and Christian tradition linked the whole Psalter to David (the Talmud says David wrote the book of Psalms with the help of ten elders, Bava Batra 14b–15a), and some readers have heard a young David being trained for kingship (119:9, 99–100) or a king in danger from his officials (119:23, 161).
views.C: Most scholars date it after the exile, in the Persian or early Greek period (roughly 500–200 BC), when the written law of Moses had become the center of Jewish life (Nehemiah 8). Its language is a mosaic of Deuteronomy, Jeremiah, Proverbs and other psalms. It mixes lament, hymn and wisdom. Some, like Jon Levenson, note that the speaker expects to be taught by God directly ("teach me", "make me understand") as well as by the written text.
views.L: Western monks spread it over the short daytime hours (Benedict assigned it to Sunday and Monday; the Roman breviary sang it every day at Prime, Terce, Sext and None until 1911). Orthodox Christians read it as Kathisma 17 at the midnight office, at Saturday matins and at funerals. Jews recite stanzas whose letters spell a dead person's name at funerals and memorials.
views.J: The Talmud calls it the "eightfold alphabet" and asks why it is not said daily instead of Psalm 145 (Berakhot 4b). Midrash Tehillim comments on many of its verses. Its lines are woven into Jewish teaching: 119:99 in the Mishnah (Avot 4:1), 119:126 in the laws of blessing (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5), 119:62 in the story of David's lyre that played at midnight (Berakhot 3b).
views.X: The New Testament does not quote it directly, but its echoes are many (John 17:17; Romans 7:12; James 1:25). Augustine and Ambrose wrote long commentaries on it, often hearing Christ, the one who kept the law perfectly, in its voice. Luther and Calvin read it as the believer's delight in God's word; Bonhoeffer left an unfinished meditation on it from 1939–1940, written for the underground seminary he led.

deep.h: The 22 letters: how the alphabet works
deep.b:
Hebrew has 22 letters. The poet gives each letter a stanza and starts all eight verses of the stanza with that letter. You can see it in the Hebrew first words below: every verse of the first stanza starts with alef (א), every verse of the second with bet (ב), and so on. Some letters have many words to choose from; others force the poet's hand. For waw (ו), which almost no Hebrew word begins with, he uses ve-, "and", eight times. For tet (ט) he uses tov, "good", five times. Letters that have two forms in Hebrew script are the same letter: sin and shin share the stanza 119:161–168.

The KJV and many printed Bibles put the letter names (ALEPH, BETH, GIMEL) over the stanzas. This site spells them alef, bet, gimel and so on throughout the Psalms. Rahlfs' Greek text prints the letter names over the stanzas in Greek letters (αλφ, βηθ, γιμελ), as many Greek and Latin manuscripts do; the transcription of Codex Sinaiticus consulted here does not show them.

The Greek and Latin use one word, entolai / mandata, for both orders and commands, so a reader of those versions sees seven words, not eight. Other words also carry the theme: "way" (derekh, 13 times), "path" ('orach, 5 times) and "faithfulness" ('emunah). Scholars disagree on whether the eight have separate meanings (law as teaching, decrees as witnessed covenant terms, orders as an overseer's instructions, rules as fixed statutes, rulings as precedents) or are used almost as one, as poetry uses synonyms. David Noel Freedman noted that eight words and eight lines per stanza seem planned together.

An often repeated claim is that every verse but one mentions God's word. Counted by the eight nouns, four do not: 119:3, 119:37, 119:90 and 119:122. Verses 3 and 37 have "way", 90 has "faithfulness", and 122 has nothing of the kind. In 119:132 the word mishpat means "what is right", not "a ruling". Meanwhile some verses have two (119:16, 43, 48, 160, 168, 172), and 119:42 has davar twice. At 119:37 some scholars think "by your word" stood in place of "in your way", but the Greek and, as reported, the Qumran scrolls agree with the Hebrew (see the variant). The scrolls do not tidy the pattern either: the Great Psalms Scroll is reported to read "your loyal love" for "your rules" at 119:83, leaving that verse with no law word. The pattern is real but not rigid, and the poet may have allowed himself the freedom.

deep.h: The text: Hebrew, Greek and the scrolls
deep.b:
Witnesses checked for this page. The Hebrew was checked in the Leningrad Codex. The Greek was checked in Rahlfs' edited text (read on bibelkommentare.de) and in Codex Sinaiticus (the Lake facsimile, read in the Source Library transcription). "The Greek" on this page means Rahlfs' text; a reading found only in Sinaiticus is named as such. The Latin readings are from the Gallican Psalter. The Dead Sea Scroll readings are reported from an English presentation of the published scroll texts (dssenglishbible.com); the scroll editions and photographs themselves were not checked.

The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex. The Greek follows the Hebrew closely but often reads the same consonants another way: milk for fat (119:70), frost for smoke (119:83), idle talk for pits (119:85), "nail down my flesh" for "my flesh bristles" (119:120), and "I have not forgotten" for "I have set" (119:30). At 119:139 it borrows "zeal for your house" from 69:9. Codex Sinaiticus alone has "your law" at 119:105 and "your ways" at 119:151. The Latin of the Gallican Psalter follows the Greek, and Christian commentary through the Middle Ages was built on that Latin. Rahlfs' text heads the psalm "Alleluia" (in Codex Sinaiticus the word comes just before the psalm number and may close Psalm 117); the Hebrew has no title, so the Plain has no verse 0.

The Dead Sea Scrolls. The Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (11QPs-a, copied in the first half of the first century AD) holds much of Psalm 119, spread over several columns with gaps where the scroll is damaged. In that scroll it comes after Psalm 132 and before Psalm 135, in an order different from the Hebrew Bible, as Peter Flint's study reports. Its text agrees mostly with the Masoretic Text. The differences reported are small, and several put a different word in the same line. At 119:83 the scroll is reported to have "you made me" for "I am" and "loyal love" for "rules"; elsewhere it has "be gracious to me" for "give me life" at 119:107, "your orders" at 119:128, and "word" for "loyal love" at 119:159. At 119:37 both 11QPs-a and 4QPs-g are reported to read "in your way" with the Hebrew, not the "by your word" some scholars have proposed. Smaller scrolls from Caves 1, 4 and 5 (among them 4QPs-g, 4QPs-h and 5QPs) preserve parts of the psalm, and some of them may have held this psalm alone.

Readers give several reasons, and they can all be true. (1) Memory: an alphabet is an index, and a 176-line poem is easier to learn if each stanza begins with the next letter. (2) Completeness: going from alef to tav says everything, the whole of devotion "from A to Z" (the rabbis used the phrase "from alef to tav" for completeness). (3) Order: a poem in strict form mirrors a law that brings order to life; C. S. Lewis compared the psalm to embroidery, done stitch by stitch out of love for the craft. (4) Teaching: alphabets were school exercises, and this one may have been written for students of the law. The eight lines per stanza match the eight law words, so the poem is built eight by eight by twenty-two.

Jewish prayer. Psalm 119 is not part of the fixed daily service, but it is read in study and private devotion. At a funeral, at the unveiling of a gravestone and on the anniversary of a death, mourners read the stanzas whose letters spell the person's Hebrew name, followed by the stanzas for the letters of neshamah (נשמה, "soul"). The custom is late and widely kept.

Western Christian prayer. Benedict's Rule (chapter 18) gives four stanzas to Prime on Sunday and three each to Terce, Sext and None on Sunday and Monday, 22 stanzas in all. The Roman breviary sang the whole psalm every day at the little hours from the early Middle Ages until 1911. The modern Liturgy of the Hours spreads its stanzas over Daytime Prayer in a four-week cycle. The Anglican Book of Common Prayer (1662) reads it over the 24th to 26th days of each month.

Eastern Christian prayer. In the Orthodox Psalter it is Kathisma 17, called the Amomos from its Greek first word ("blameless"). It is read at the midnight office, at Saturday matins and at funerals and memorial services, where verses of it alternate with the refrain "Alleluia". At the matins of Holy Saturday the Lamentations at Christ's tomb are sung between its verses.

settings.what: Opening blessings on those who walk by the law
settings.by: the psalmist, speaking as a teacher
settings.to: those who hear or read the psalm, especially the young (compare 119:9)
settings.when: no title gives an occasion; it is the doorway to the prayer that follows
settings.why: to hold up the goal before the hearer, as Psalm 1 does: a life that walks by the LORD's law is the happy life. Everything after this is the speaker's own struggle to live it.
settings.readers: Jews after the exile, gathered around the written law (Nehemiah 8), heard here the promise that devotion to the law is the way to life.

settings.what: A long prayer to God about his word
settings.by: "your servant", a devout Israelite who loves God's law, under pressure from the arrogant and from officials
settings.to: the LORD, spoken to as "you" in every verse except 119:115, where the speaker turns to evildoers
settings.when: a time of mockery, false charges and danger to life (119:23, 51, 69, 78, 85–87, 109, 161), perhaps under foreign rule
settings.why: to hold on to God's word when everything else fails, to ask to be taught, kept alive and rescued, and to give learners a model of how to pray the law. Knowing the speaker is in trouble keeps the poem from being a dry list of rules: it is love of the law under pressure.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying alone or together, learned from it to treat the law as a living word and to bring every need to God through it.
views: Most scholars: a learned devout Jew of the Persian or Greek period, perhaps a teacher of the young (119:9, 99).
Will Soll: a lament in the voice of King Jehoiachin in Babylon, the Davidic king who hopes to be restored by keeping the law (2 Kings 25:27–30).
Kent Reynolds: an ideal portrait of the Torah student, written to shape learners.
Some readers: the people in exile, a foreigner on the earth with only God's word for its inheritance (119:19, 111).

traditions.q: The psalmist delights in the law of Moses. What place does that law have in a Christian's life?
views: The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still binds believers as a rule of life, though not as a way to earn salvation; the ceremonial laws are fulfilled in Christ and the civil laws expired with Israel's state (Westminster Confession 19). Calvin calls teaching believers God's will the law's principal use and points to David's delight in it (Institutes 2.7.12).

Law and gospel must be kept distinct: the law shows sin and drives to Christ, and it always accuses. Because believers are still sinners, they also need the law as a guide (the "third use", Formula of Concord 6), but good works come from the Spirit freely, not from the law's pressure. Lutherans themselves debate how much weight the third use carries.

The Old Law is holy and good, a first stage of revelation that prepares for the Gospel; the New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit given through faith in Christ, which fulfills and perfects it. The moral precepts of the Ten Commandments remain binding as expressions of the natural law (Catechism 1961–1974; 2068–2070).

The law of Moses was given to Israel as a rule of life for a past dispensation. Christians are not under it but under grace and the law of Christ; its moral content applies where the New Testament repeats it (Romans 6:14; 1 Corinthians 9:21).

The Ten Commandments, including the seventh-day Sabbath, bind all people in every age. Obedience is the fruit of salvation by grace, not its cause, and Psalm 119's love of the law is the Christian's pattern (Fundamental Beliefs 19).
